a: Ten shares in the king belong to us.
t: "We are the firstborn"
p: The Greek adds that the northern tribes claimed to be the firstborn, and it also keeps the Hebrew's "even in David."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
readings.orig: עֶשֶׂר יָדוֹת לִי בַמֶּלֶךְ וְגַם־בְּדָוִד אֲנִי מִמְּךָ
readings.en: ten hands are mine in the king, and also in David I more than you
readings.plain: Ten shares in the king belong to us.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (kaige-revised Greek) and Lucianic (Antiochene) Greek manuscripts, as reported (Rahlfs edition)
readings.en: and I am firstborn rather than you
readings.plain: Ten shares in the king belong to us, and we are the firstborn, not you.

why: The Hebrew makes good sense as it stands. The Greek clause probably reflects a Hebrew text with bekhor, "firstborn," instead of (or beside) beDavid, "in David"; the two words look alike in Hebrew script. Some scholars, such as McCarter, prefer the Greek because Israel's claim to be the firstborn (Reuben, then Joseph, 1 Chronicles 5:1–2) fits a quarrel over rank. The Plain English keeps the Hebrew and shows the Greek here.
b: Note on the Greek of these chapters: from 2 Samuel 11:2 to 1 Kings 2:11, Codex Vaticanus (and so Rahlfs' printed edition, which follows it) carries a revision, called kaige, that brought the Greek closer to the Hebrew. All of 2 Samuel 19–24 lies inside that section. The Lucianic (Antiochene) manuscripts are the better witness to the Old Greek here, so each Greek reading on these pages says which of the two it comes from.

a: All the Berites
t: Berites, Bichrites, or chosen men?
p: No people called "Berites" is known. Many modern translations change it to "Bichrites," Sheba's clan.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, BSB
readings.plain: All the Berites

readings.w: Emendation to habbikri, the clan of Bichri; NIV ("Bikrites"), ESV and NRSV ("Bichrites")
readings.plain: All the Bichrites

readings.w: Latin Vulgate, omnes electi, which seems to read habbachurim
readings.plain: All the chosen men

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (kaige-revised Greek), as reported
readings.plain: All in Charri

why: "Bichrites" fits the story well: Sheba son of Bichri rallies his own clan. But it is a scholar's correction with no manuscript behind it. The Vulgate's "chosen men" points to a different Hebrew word, and the Greek of Vaticanus has a place name, Charri, that is no clearer. Since no reading is certain, the Plain English keeps the Hebrew; the note on this verse discusses the problem.

a: 'Be sure to ask at Abel,' and that was how things got finished.
t: The proverb about Abel
p: The Greek gives a longer proverb: ask at Abel and at Dan whether the customs of Israel's faithful have failed.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
readings.en: surely they will ask at Abel, and so they finished
readings.plain: 'Be sure to ask at Abel,' and that was how things got finished.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (kaige-revised Greek) and Lucianic (Antiochene) Greek manuscripts, as reported
readings.orig: ἐν τῇ Αβελ καὶ ἐν Δαν εἰ ἐξέλιπον ἃ ἔθεντο οἱ πιστοὶ τοῦ Ισραηλ
readings.en: in Abel and in Dan, whether the things that the faithful of Israel set down have failed
readings.plain: 'Ask at Abel and at Dan whether what Israel's faithful ones laid down has come to an end,' and that was how things got finished.

why: The Hebrew is short but clear: Abel was known for wise answers that settled disputes. The Greek's longer saying seems to reflect a Hebrew text with "Dan" and with words like those in 20:19 ("faithful ones of Israel"); some scholars (McCarter) think it is original and that the Hebrew lost words. Because it may also be an expansion based on 20:19, the Plain English keeps the Hebrew.

a: Kerethites
t: Kerethites or Carians?
p: The written Hebrew has "Kari," perhaps Carians; the scribes' reading is "Kerethites."

readings.w: Masoretic Text, scribes' reading (Qere); KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
readings.plain: Kerethites

readings.w: Masoretic Text, written text (Ketiv)
readings.plain: Carians

why: Everywhere else David's guard is "the Kerethites and the Pelethites" (8:18; 15:18; 1 Kings 1:38), so the scribes read the familiar word. The written form "Kari" appears in 2 Kings 11:4 and 11:19 for the royal guard of a later time, and may mean Carians, mercenaries from southwest Asia Minor. The written text here may reflect that later name.

a: at Gibeah of Saul, the LORD's chosen one
t: Gibeah or Gibeon? Chosen one or mountain?
p: The Hebrew says "at Gibeah of Saul, the LORD's chosen." The Greek says "in Gibeon," and the NRSV also reads "the mountain of the LORD."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
readings.en: in Gibeah of Saul, the chosen of the LORD
readings.plain: at Gibeah of Saul, the LORD's chosen one

readings.w: Greek (Codex Vaticanus (kaige-revised Greek) and Lucianic (Antiochene) Greek manuscripts, as reported)
readings.en: in Gibeon of Saul, chosen ones of the Lord
readings.plain: at Gibeon of Saul, as chosen ones of the LORD

readings.w: Greek "Gibeon" with the emendation behar YHWH, "on the mountain of the LORD," for bechir YHWH; NRSV
readings.en: at Gibeon on the mountain of the LORD
readings.plain: at Gibeon on the mountain of the LORD

why: Gibeon was the Gibeonites' own town and had a famous high place (1 Kings 3:4), so executing the men there "before the LORD" makes sense, and 21:9 says they died "on the hill" (or "mountain") "before the LORD." "Mountain" and "chosen" differ by one letter in Hebrew (har, bechir). Gibeah, though, was Saul's home town, and the Hebrew reading may be pointed on purpose. The Plain English keeps the Hebrew.

a: Merab
t: Michal or Merab?
p: The Hebrew says "Michal," but Michal had no children and Adriel was Merab's husband.

readings.w: Two Hebrew manuscripts and some Greek manuscripts (Lucianic); NIV, ESV, NRSV, BSB
readings.plain: Merab

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, Vulgate
readings.plain: Michal

readings.w: Targum Jonathan (Aramaic paraphrase), as reported by Harrington and Saldarini: a conflation of both names
readings.orig: (both names; Aramaic text in Harrington and Saldarini)
readings.en: the sons of Merab, whom Michal brought up
readings.plain: Merab, whom Michal brought up,

why: Saul's elder daughter Merab was promised to David but given to "Adriel the Meholathite" (1 Samuel 18:19), and Michal "had no child to the day of her death" (6:23). The names are easy to confuse in a list of Saul's family. The Talmud keeps "Michal" and explains that Merab bore the sons but Michal raised them (Bavli Sanhedrin 19b), and the Targum writes both names into the verse in the same sense; the King James Version, following the Hebrew, says Michal "brought up" the sons. The Plain English follows the reading that fits the rest of Samuel.

a: Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim the Bethlehemite struck down Goliath the Gittite
t: Elhanan and Goliath
p: Samuel says Elhanan killed Goliath. Chronicles says he killed Goliath's brother Lahmi. The Targum makes Elhanan David.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Greek (Codex Vaticanus (kaige-revised Greek), as reported); ESV, NRSV (the KJV adds "the brother of" in italics)
readings.orig: וַיַּךְ אֶלְחָנָן בֶּן־יַעְרֵי אֹרְגִים בֵּית הַלַּחְמִי אֵת גָּלְיָת הַגִּתִּי
readings.en: and Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim the Bethlehemite struck Goliath the Gittite
readings.plain: Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim the Bethlehemite struck down Goliath the Gittite

readings.w: Parallel text, 1 Chronicles 20:5 (Masoretic Text); the BSB and NIV follow it, giving "son of Jair" and "the brother of Goliath"
readings.orig: וַיַּךְ אֶלְחָנָן בֶּן־יָעִור אֶת־לַחְמִי אֲחִי גָּלְיָת הַגִּתִּי
readings.en: and Elhanan son of Jair struck Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite
readings.plain: Elhanan son of Jair struck down Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite

readings.w: Targum Jonathan (Aramaic paraphrase)
readings.orig: ומחא דוד בר ישי... ית גלית גתאה
readings.en: and David son of Jesse... struck Goliath the Gittite
readings.plain: David son of Jesse, the weaver of the sanctuary curtains, from Bethlehem, struck down Goliath the Gittite

why: The Hebrew of Samuel is the harder reading, and the Greek supports it. Chronicles' text can be explained as a careful reading of damaged letters: the Hebrew for "the Bethlehemite, Goliath" (beit hallachmi et golyat) contains the letters of "Lahmi the brother of Goliath" (lachmi achi golyat). Many scholars think Chronicles either preserves a better text or harmonized with 1 Samuel 17. "Jaare-oregim" has probably picked up oregim, "weavers," from the end of the verse; Chronicles' "Jair" is likely the original name. The Plain English translates Samuel's text and gives the others here; the note on this verse lays out the views.

a: The God of my rock
t: "God of my rock" or "my God, my rock"?
p: Samuel's Hebrew says "the God of my rock." Psalm 18:2 has "my God, my rock," which many translations use here too.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) of 2 Samuel; KJV
readings.plain: The God of my rock

readings.w: Psalm 18:2 (Masoretic Text); NIV, ESV, BSB in 2 Samuel
readings.plain: My God, my rock

why: "The God of my rock" probably means "God, who is my rock." The Psalm's "my God, my rock" is smoother, and translators often bring it into Samuel. Samuel's verse is also longer than the Psalm's: its last lines, "my safe place, my rescuer; from violence you rescue me," have no match in Psalm 18:2. The Plain English keeps Samuel's text.

a: the base of the heavens shuddered
t: Heavens or mountains?
p: Samuel's copy of the song has "heavens"; Psalm 18:7 has "mountains."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) of 2 Samuel
readings.plain: the base of the heavens shuddered

readings.w: Psalm 18:7 (Masoretic Text)
readings.plain: the base of the mountains shuddered

why: Both make sense: the mountains were thought to hold up the sky (Job 26:11). The Psalm's "earth... mountains" is a more common pair, so Samuel's "heavens" is the less expected reading and may be original. The Plain English follows Samuel's own text throughout this chapter and gives the Psalm's readings in notes and variants.

a: he came into view on the wind's wings
t: Seen, or soaring?
p: Samuel says the LORD "was seen" on the wings of the wind. Psalm 18:10 says he "swooped."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) of 2 Samuel; KJV, ESV
readings.plain: he came into view on the wind's wings

readings.w: Psalm 18:10 (Masoretic Text), and reportedly some Hebrew manuscripts of Samuel; NIV, BSB
readings.plain: he swooped down on the wind's wings

why: The Hebrew letters dalet (d) and resh (r) look almost alike, and the two verbs differ only by them. "He swooped" (yede', used of an eagle in Deuteronomy 28:49 and Jeremiah 48:40) fits a flying cherub better, and many scholars think it is original. But "he was seen" also makes sense in a theophany, and it is Samuel's reading; the Plain English keeps it and shows the Psalm's verb here.

a: God is my fortress of strength
t: Fortress, or the God who arms me?
p: Samuel's Hebrew reads "God is my strong fortress." Psalm 18:32 and the Greek of Samuel have "the God who arms me with strength."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) of 2 Samuel; KJV, ESV, BSB
readings.en: God is my fortress of strength
readings.plain: God is my fortress of strength

readings.w: Psalm 18:32 (Masoretic Text); the Greek of Samuel (Codex Vaticanus (kaige-revised Greek), ho krataion me dynamei, "who strengthens me with power"); 4QSam-a commonly reported to agree with the Psalm; NIV
readings.en: the God who girds me with strength
readings.plain: God is the one who wraps me in strength

why: The Psalm's reading matches the picture of a warrior armed by God in 22:35 and 22:40 ("You wrapped me in strength for battle"), and many scholars prefer it. Samuel's reading is also good Hebrew and fits the list of fortresses in 22:2–3. The second line differs too: Samuel has vayyatter, "he set free" (the Plain's "free and whole"), and the Psalm has vayyitten, "he made" (my way whole). In that line the written Hebrew (Ketiv) has "his way" and the scribes' reading (Qere) "my way"; the Plain English follows the Qere. The Plain English keeps Samuel's text and gives the Psalm's here.
b: The 4QSam-a agreement is reported in secondary literature; I could not confirm it in DJD 17.

a: when you answer me, you make me great
t: Your answering, or your gentleness?
p: Samuel says God's "answering" makes the king great; Psalm 18:35 says God's "gentleness" does, and adds a line.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) of 2 Samuel
readings.en: and your answering makes me great
readings.plain: when you answer me, you make me great

readings.w: Psalm 18:35 (Masoretic Text)
readings.en: your right hand supports me, and your humility makes me great
readings.plain: your right hand holds me up; your gentleness makes me great

why: The two key words, 'anotkha and 'anvatkha, differ by one letter. The Psalm's "gentleness" or "humility" is the bolder idea and may be original; Samuel's "answering" may be a simpler reading of the same letters. The Psalm's extra line, "your right hand holds me up," is missing in Samuel. The Plain English follows Samuel.

a: He makes great the rescues of his king
t: Tower or "makes great"?
p: The written Hebrew says God "makes great" his king's rescues, as Psalm 18:50 does. The scribes read "a tower."

readings.w: Masoretic Text, written text (Ketiv) of Samuel; Psalm 18:50; Greek (Codex Vaticanus (kaige-revised Greek)); NIV, ESV, BSB
readings.en: making great the rescues of his king
readings.plain: He makes great the rescues of his king

readings.w: Masoretic Text, scribes' reading (Qere) of Samuel; KJV
readings.en: a tower of rescues for his king
readings.plain: He is a tower of rescues for his king

why: The two readings differ in vowels and in one consonant: yod in magdil, "making great," and vav in migdol, "tower." The written text agrees with Psalm 18:50 and the Greek, so the Plain English follows it. The scribes' "tower" fits the song's fortress imagery and is the reading behind the King James Version's "He is the tower of salvation for his king." Jewish liturgy uses both: the grace after meals reads "tower" on Sabbaths and festivals and "makes great" on weekdays.

a: the man set up on high
t: "Set up on high" or "whom God raised up"?
p: The Hebrew reads "the man raised on high." 4QSam-a and the Greek seem to read "the man God raised up."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
readings.plain: the man set up on high

readings.w: Dead Sea Scroll 4QSam-a as reported (Ulrich; McCarter), and the Greek (Codex Vaticanus (kaige-revised Greek), as reported, "whom the Lord raised up"); NRSV ("the man whom God exalted")
readings.plain: the man God raised up

why: The two readings differ in a consonant ('ayin in 'al, "on high"; aleph in 'el, "God") and in the form of the verb. Both make the same point, that David did not raise himself. The scroll reading is attractive and the NRSV follows it, but I could not check the scroll's letters myself, so the Plain English keeps the Masoretic Text.
b: The 4QSam-a reading is given as reported; it could not be checked in DJD 17.

a: He was Adino the Eznite; eight hundred fell at his hand at one time.
t: "Adino the Eznite" or "he wielded his spear"?
p: The Hebrew names "Adino the Eznite." Most modern translations restore "he wielded his spear" from 1 Chronicles 11:11.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.orig: הוּא עֲדִינוֹ הָעֶצְנִי עַל־שְׁמֹנֶה מֵאוֹת חָלָל בְּפַעַם אֶחָת
readings.en: he, Adino the Eznite, over eight hundred slain at one time
readings.plain: He was Adino the Eznite; eight hundred fell at his hand at one time.

readings.w: Restored from 1 Chronicles 11:11 (which reads "three hundred"); NIV, ESV, NRSV, BSB; the KJV gives the names and adds "he lift up his spear" in italics
readings.en: he raised his spear over eight hundred
readings.plain: He swung his spear over eight hundred, slain at one time.

why: "Adino the Eznite" is found nowhere else, and the line lacks a verb, so most scholars think the text is damaged and that Chronicles' "he raised his spear" (compare Abishai in 23:18) shows what it once said. Codex Vaticanus (kaige) has the names and also a verb: Adinon ho Asonaios; houtos espasato ten hromphaian autou epi oktakosious, "Adino the Asonite; he drew his sword against eight hundred," which may combine both. The written Hebrew (Ketiv) of "the Eznite" is ha'etsno, a form the STEPBible data glosses "his spear," which is part of the case that the name hides a word for a weapon. Because the Hebrew can be read as it stands and the restoration is a guess about lost letters, the Plain English keeps it and gives the restoration here. Chronicles' count of three hundred may be a copying change, or influenced by 23:18.

a: Josheb-basshebeth the Tahchemonite
t: Josheb-basshebeth, Ishbaal, or Jashobeam?
p: The Hebrew name means "sitting in the seat." The Lucianic Greek has "Iesbaal" (Ishbaal); Chronicles has "Jashobeam."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV (as a description), NIV, ESV, NRSV, BSB
readings.plain: Josheb-basshebeth the Tahchemonite

readings.w: Lucianic (Antiochene) Greek manuscripts, as reported
readings.plain: Ishbaal the Tahchemonite

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (kaige-revised Greek), as reported
readings.plain: Ish-bosheth the Tahchemonite

readings.w: 1 Chronicles 11:11 (Masoretic Text)
readings.plain: Jashobeam son of Hachmoni

why: The Lucianic "Iesbaal" is the main witness for the theory that the man was called Ishbaal and that scribes replaced baal with bosheth, "shame" (see the note). Vaticanus shows the replaced form. Chronicles has a different form again. Because the Hebrew is the received text and the original name is uncertain, the Plain English keeps it.

a: chief of the Three
t: Chief of the Three, or of the officers?
p: The Hebrew hashshalishi can be read "the Three" or "the officers" (the KJV's "captains").

readings.w: Masoretic Text read as "the Three"; NIV, ESV, NRSV, BSB
readings.plain: chief of the Three

readings.w: The same Hebrew read as shalish, "officer"; KJV ("chief among the captains"); Codex Vaticanus (kaige-revised Greek), as reported, "chief of the third"
readings.plain: chief of the officers

why: There is no Ketiv and Qere here; the problem is the one ambiguous word. "The Three" fits the list that follows (23:9, 23:18–19, 23:22–23), where the Three are a named group, so the Plain English reads it that way. "Officers" is also a real word (Exodus 14:7; 2 Kings 10:25).

a: At harvest
t: At harvest, or to the rock?
p: Samuel says the three came "at harvest." 1 Chronicles 11:15 says they came "to the rock."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, ESV, NRSV, BSB
readings.plain: At harvest

readings.w: 1 Chronicles 11:15 (Masoretic Text)
readings.plain: To the rock

why: The Hebrew words look alike (qatsir, hatstsur). "To the rock" fits the cave and the hill country; "at harvest" dates the story and fits Philistine raids on the harvest (compare 1 Samuel 23:1). Both are possible. The Plain English keeps Samuel's reading.

a: head of the Thirty
t: Head of the Three or of the Thirty?
p: The Hebrew says Abishai was chief of "the three" (written "the third"). The Syriac and two manuscripts say "the Thirty."

readings.w: Syriac Peshitta and two Hebrew manuscripts; NRSV, ESV
readings.plain: head of the Thirty

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (Ketiv "the third," Qere "the three"); KJV, NIV, BSB
readings.plain: head of the Three

why: The passage says Abishai "never came up to the Three" (23:19), so he cannot have been their chief. "Head of the Thirty" makes the passage consistent, and the three/thirty confusion happens several times in this list (23:13, 23:19; 1 Chronicles 11:20–21). The NIV, BSB and KJV keep "the Three" and suppose Abishai led a second group of three. Because the Plain follows "the Thirty," it also reads "the Thirty" in 23:19 (see that variant), and it renders the end of this verse, "he had a name among the Three," as "he was famous alongside the Three": known with them, not one of them.

a: Of the Thirty he was the most honored, was he not?
t: The Three or the Thirty, again
p: The Hebrew says Abishai was "honored above the Three." Reading "the Thirty" here matches 23:18 and 23:23.

readings.w: Correction to "the Thirty," matching 23:18 and 23:23; NRSV
readings.en: of the thirty, was he not honored?
readings.plain: Of the Thirty he was the most honored, was he not?

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, BSB
readings.en: more than the three, was he not honored?
readings.plain: Of the Three he was the most honored, was he not?

why: Read as it stands, the verse says Abishai was more honored than the Three and their captain, yet never came up to the Three, which is hard to make sense of. 23:23 says the same of Benaiah with "the Thirty" in the first half. The parallel, 1 Chronicles 11:20–21, is itself confused. With "the Thirty" in 23:18, the Plain reads "the Thirty" here too, so that Abishai leads the Thirty but does not reach the Three. This is a correction with little manuscript support, so the Hebrew is given here.

a: the two lion-men of Moab
t: Lion-men, or sons of Ariel?
p: The Hebrew has the obscure word 'ari'el. The Greek reads "the two sons of Ariel of Moab," and the NRSV follows it.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV ("two lionlike men"), NIV and BSB ("champions")
readings.plain: the two lion-men of Moab

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (kaige-revised Greek), as reported; NRSV
readings.orig: τοὺς δύο υἱοὺς Αριηλ τοῦ Μωαβ
readings.en: the two sons of Ariel of Moab
readings.plain: the two sons of Ariel of Moab

why: The Greek may have supplied "sons" to make sense of a hard word, or it may preserve a lost bene, "sons of." Earlier in the verse there is a Ketiv and Qere as well: the written text calls Benaiah "son of a living man" (chai), and the scribes read "son of a man of strength" (chayil); the Plain's "a fighter's son" follows the scribes' reading. The note on this verse discusses what an ariel was.

a: son of Shammah the Hararite;
t: Jonathan son of Shammah, or Jonathan and Shammah?
p: The Hebrew has no "son of" here, so it lists "Jonathan, Shammah the Hararite" as two men. The Plain adds "son of," as the Greek does.

readings.w: Greek (Lucianic (Antiochene) Greek manuscripts, as reported), as restored in the BHS apparatus; NIV, NRSV, BSB
readings.plain: son of Shammah the Hararite;

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV
readings.plain: Shammah the Hararite;

readings.w: 1 Chronicles 11:34 (Masoretic Text)
readings.plain: son of Shagee the Hararite;

why: Shammah the Hararite has already been named among the Three (23:11), so listing him again among the Thirty is odd, and Chronicles has "Jonathan son of Shagee the Hararite." Most scholars therefore read "Jonathan son of Shammah," the son of the hero of 23:11. The word "son of" is not in the Leningrad Codex; it is supplied from the Greek, and the STEPBible data used on this site lists it as such an added word (kind "X"). The Plain follows the restoration. The choice changes the count in 23:39 by one name.

a: Joab, commander of the army, who was with him
t: Joab alone, or Joab and the commanders?
p: The Hebrew says the king spoke to "Joab, commander of the army." The Lucianic Greek and 1 Chronicles 21:2 add "and the commanders."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, ESV, BSB
readings.en: to Joab, commander of the army, who was with him
readings.plain: Joab, commander of the army, who was with him

readings.w: Lucianic (Antiochene) Greek manuscripts, as reported; compare 1 Chronicles 21:2; NIV, NRSV
readings.orig: πρὸς Ιωαβ καὶ πρὸς τοὺς ἄρχοντας τῆς δυνάμεως
readings.en: to Joab and to the commanders of the army
readings.plain: Joab and the commanders of the army who were with him

why: The longer reading fits 24:4, where "Joab and the commanders of the army" go out together, and it may be original; the Hebrew "who was with him" is singular, which suits the shorter text. Vaticanus (kaige) agrees with the Hebrew here, as the kaige revision usually does. The Plain English keeps the Hebrew.

a: set up camp in Aroer
t: Camped at Aroer, or began from Aroer?
p: The Hebrew says the officers camped at Aroer. The Lucianic Greek says they began from Aroer.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Codex Vaticanus (kaige-revised Greek), as reported; KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
readings.plain: set up camp in Aroer

readings.w: Lucianic (Antiochene) Greek manuscripts, as reported; NRSV
readings.plain: began from Aroer

why: "They began from Aroer" suits a description of a route and needs only a small change in the Hebrew verb (vayyachellu for vayyachanu). The Lucianic text is the better Old Greek witness in these chapters, which gives the reading weight. But "camped" also makes sense for a team that spent nearly ten months on the road. The Plain English keeps the Hebrew.

a: the land of Tahtim-hodshi
t: Tahtim-hodshi or Kadesh of the Hittites?
p: The unknown name may be a damaged form of "the land of the Hittites, Kadesh," as some Greek manuscripts read.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
readings.plain: the land of Tahtim-hodshi

readings.w: Lucianic (Antiochene) Greek manuscripts, as reported; NRSV
readings.en: to the land of the Hittites, Kadesh
readings.plain: Kadesh in the land of the Hittites

why: No place called Tahtim-hodshi is known, and the Greek reading points to Kadesh on the Orontes River, far to the north in Syria, which some think marked the edge of David's influence. Others think Kadesh is too far north for an Israelite count. Since the Greek may itself be a guess at a hard text, the Plain English keeps the Hebrew name.
b: Codex Vaticanus (kaige) has a different, also obscure, name here; the Kadesh reading is the Lucianic one.

a: seven years
t: Seven years of famine, or three?
p: The Hebrew says seven years. The Greek and 1 Chronicles 21:12 say three, matching three months and three days.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV
readings.plain: seven years

readings.w: Greek (Codex Vaticanus (kaige-revised Greek) and Lucianic (Antiochene) Greek manuscripts, as reported); 1 Chronicles 21:12; NIV, ESV, NRSV, BSB
readings.plain: three years

why: "Three years, three months, three days" is a neat pattern, and the Greek and Chronicles have it. That neatness could be original, or a later scribe could have smoothed "seven" into the pattern. Seven is the harder reading. Jewish commentators such as Radak, following rabbinic sources, reconcile the two: three famine years had already passed in the Gibeonite story (21:1), three more were now threatened, and the year between, before the next harvest, made a seventh, so Chronicles counts only the new three. The Plain English keeps the Hebrew and shows the other reading.

a: from morning until the set time
t: Until the set time, or until midday?
p: The Greek says the plague lasted "until the hour of the midday meal" and adds that David chose it at wheat harvest.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
readings.en: from the morning until the time of the appointment
readings.plain: from morning until the set time

readings.w: Greek: Codex Vaticanus (kaige-revised Greek) and Lucianic (Antiochene) Greek manuscripts alike
readings.en: from morning until the hour of the midday meal
readings.plain: from morning until the hour of the midday meal

why: The Hebrew "set time" probably means the end of the three days God had named (24:13), though it is a strange phrase. The Greek reading would mean the plague was cut short on its first day, which fits God's stopping it in 24:16. The Greek also begins the verse with "And David chose the death for himself; it was the days of the wheat harvest." Some scholars think the Greek shows a Hebrew text that had these words. Because the plus is in both the kaige text and the Lucianic text, it is probably Old Greek. The Plain English follows the Hebrew.
b: Note on the Greek of these chapters: from 2 Samuel 11:2 to 1 Kings 2:11, Codex Vaticanus (and so Rahlfs' printed edition, which follows it) carries a revision, called kaige, that brought the Greek closer to the Hebrew. All of 2 Samuel 19–24 lies inside that section. The Lucianic (Antiochene) manuscripts are the better witness to the Old Greek here, so each Greek reading on these pages says which of the two it comes from.

a: The LORD's angel was close to the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.
t: The angel with the drawn sword
p: The Dead Sea scroll 4QSam-a seems to have had a longer text here, like 1 Chronicles 21:16: David sees the angel with a sword over Jerusalem.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Greek (Codex Vaticanus (kaige-revised Greek) and Lucianic (Antiochene) Greek manuscripts); KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
readings.orig: וּמַלְאַךְ יְהוָה הָיָה עִם־גֹּרֶן הָאֲרַוְנָה הַיְבֻסִי
readings.en: and the angel of the LORD was by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite
readings.plain: The LORD's angel was close to the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.

readings.w: Dead Sea Scroll 4QSam-a (about 50–25 BC), as reported; the wording is reconstructed after 1 Chronicles 21:16, and how much of it the fragments preserve is debated
readings.en: ...David looked up and saw the angel of the LORD standing between earth and heaven, with his sword drawn in his hand, stretched out over Jerusalem. And the elders, covered in sackcloth, fell on their faces...
readings.plain: The LORD's angel was close to the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite. David looked up and saw the LORD's angel standing between earth and sky, his sword drawn in his hand, stretched out over Jerusalem. And the elders, covered in sackcloth, fell on their faces.

why: This is one of the best-known places where 4QSam-a is thought to agree with Chronicles against the Masoretic Text. Only parts of a few lines survive, and the scene is filled out from Chronicles. Ulrich and McCarter took the fragments to show that the scroll had the whole plus. Frank Moore Cross (2006) offered a new reconstruction of these lines, and Innocent Himbaza (2010) re-examined how much is actually legible and warned against building too much on it, including in Bible translations. One reported detail is the scroll's word for the elders' dress, "covered" (mitkassim) in sackcloth, against Chronicles' "clothed" (mekhussim). If the plus was there, the shorter Masoretic Text may have lost it when a scribe's eye skipped between similar phrases; others think the longer text was expanded. The Plain English follows the Masoretic Text, as all major translations do.
b: This report rests on published discussions of 4QSam-a (Ulrich 1978; McCarter 1984; Cross 2006; Himbaza 2010; the translation in Abegg, Flint and Ulrich 1999; Tov). I could not consult the official edition (DJD 17) directly, so I give no Hebrew for the scroll: the English above is the reconstruction as reported, not a transcription of preserved letters.

a: it is I who sinned, I who did wrong
t: "I the shepherd"
p: The Greek, and reportedly 4QSam-a, read "I the shepherd did wrong," setting the shepherd against the sheep.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, ESV
readings.en: I have sinned, and I have done wrong
readings.plain: it is I who sinned, I who did wrong

readings.w: Greek (Codex Vaticanus (kaige-revised Greek) and Lucianic (Antiochene) Greek manuscripts, as reported); 4QSam-a as reported (haro'eh hare'oti); NIV, BSB
readings.orig: καὶ ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν ἐκακοποίησα
readings.en: and I the shepherd did evil
readings.plain: it is I who sinned, I the shepherd who did wrong

readings.w: 1 Chronicles 21:17 (Masoretic Text)
readings.en: and I have surely done evil
readings.plain: it is I who sinned and did great evil

why: The scroll is reported to read haro'eh hare'oti, "I the shepherd did wrong," where the Masoretic Text has ve'anokhi he'eviti, "and I did wrong." In the scroll's reading the two words look and sound alike, so one could easily have been dropped, or added by echo. Chronicles' vehara' hare'oti, "I have surely done evil," looks like another way of reading the same letters as "the shepherd did evil." The shepherd fits the next words, "these sheep," very well, and many scholars think it original. The Plain English follows the Masoretic Text and shows the other readings. The STEPBible word list used on this site marks "the shepherd" as a word added from another witness.
b: The 4QSam-a reading is given as reported by Ulrich and McCarter; it could not be checked in DJD 17.

a: Araunah looked down
t: Araunah threshing wheat, and servants in sackcloth
p: 4QSam-a is reported to add, as 1 Chronicles 21:20 does, that Araunah was threshing wheat, and that the king's servants came covered in sackcloth.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Greek (Codex Vaticanus (kaige-revised Greek) and Lucianic (Antiochene) Greek manuscripts); KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
readings.plain: Araunah looked down

readings.w: Dead Sea Scroll 4QSam-a, as reported; largely reconstructed after 1 Chronicles 21:20, and called speculative in the Dead Sea Scrolls Bible translation
readings.orig: (reconstructed; the scroll spells the name ארנא, Arna)
readings.en: Arna was threshing wheat... the king and his servants coming toward him, covered in sackcloth
readings.plain: Araunah was threshing wheat. Araunah looked down

why: Published studies report that 4QSam-a has words about Araunah (spelled "Arna") threshing wheat, like Chronicles, and a second plus later in the verse: the king's servants approach "covered in sackcloth," like the elders of the plus after 24:16. The scroll is broken, and the wording and placement are restored. Cross (2006) and Himbaza (2010) disagree about how much of this can be read. If the readings stand, they are another sign that the Chronicler used a Samuel text like the scroll's. The Masoretic Text and the Greek lack the words, and the Plain English follows them.
b: This variant rests on reports in Ulrich (1978), McCarter (1984), Cross (2006), Himbaza (2010) and the Dead Sea Scrolls Bible; I could not check the letters in DJD 17, so no reconstructed Hebrew is given.

a: and the plague was held back from Israel.
t: Solomon enlarges the altar
p: The Greek adds a last sentence: Solomon later made David's altar bigger, because it was small at first.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
readings.en: and the plague was held back from Israel
readings.plain: and the plague was held back from Israel.

readings.w: Greek: Codex Vaticanus (kaige-revised Greek) and Lucianic (Antiochene) Greek manuscripts, as reported
readings.orig: καὶ προσέθηκεν Σαλωμων ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιαστήριον ἐπ' ἐσχάτῳ, ὅτι μικρὸν ἦν ἐν πρώτοις
readings.en: and Solomon added to the altar at the end, for it was small at first
readings.plain: and the plague was held back from Israel. Later Solomon enlarged the altar, because at first it was small.

why: The Greek sentence ties the book's ending to Solomon's temple, the link Chronicles makes openly (1 Chronicles 22:1). It is most likely an explanatory addition by a later scribe or translator, and it is not in any Hebrew witness known. The Plain English follows the Hebrew.
